day_1.utterance: Come on! Let's get everything useful over here — move it!
day_1.response: Yea alright. What are we working with?

day_1.utterance: I thought we were going to die. Did you get that feeling… like your mind just went completely blank?
day_1.response: Yea. That's what it does. Give the thought a pause and then get up. We're not dead yet, eh.

day_1.utterance: *Sits silently against the wreckage, staring into the distance, not moving, not saying a word.*
day_1.response: He'll come around. Let him be.

day_1.utterance: First-aid kit is good for three days. Two bottles of water. Food is basically nothing.
day_1.response: Right. So water is the immediate problem. Food you can go without for weeks. Water, not so long. What's the terrain like around us — do we hear anything? Running water nearby is worth more than anything else in that pile.

day_1.utterance: Inventory's done. Priorities in order: water, shelter, signal.
day_1.response: Agreed on the priorities. Signal first or water first is the question tho. That radio — is it functional? Because if it is, you put out a signal *before* you go anywhere. Someone needs to stay with it and keep trying. You don't want to be half a mile into the trees when someone's listening.

day_1.utterance: So — how do we split the blankets?
day_1.response: Michelangelo gets one. He's already shaken up and cold won't help that. The other one — whoever's taking first watch doesn't need it as much as the one sleeping. So figure out the watch rotation and the blanket follows from that.

day_2.utterance: Freshwater source is to the northeast — two hours on foot. Someone has to go tomorrow. You or DaVinci?
day_2.response: I'll go. DaVinci stays here with the radio and keeps Michelangelo from spiraling. That's the better use of resources. Two hours northeast — what am I looking for exactly, and is there anything between here and there I should know about?

day_2.utterance: Today's tasks: collect fresh water, patch the weak spots in camp, sort the first-aid kit. I'll handle the water. You and DaVinci split the other two.
day_2.response: Hold on. You said I was going for the water. Now you're saying you'll handle it? Which is it? Make up your mind and stick to it — we don't want two people heading northeast and nobody minding the camp. Pick a lane.

day_2.utterance: I… I can't find my stuff. The gauze from the first-aid kit — have you seen it?
day_2.response: No, I haven't touched it. Check where you last had it. But while I have you — that empty bottle next to Donatello's rationing plan. You put it there on purpose, yea? What are you thinking about that?

day_2.utterance: Before Donatello came back just now… I saw her put a pack of crackers into her own bag. What do you think we should do?
day_2.response:
Well. That's two things now, isn't it. The bottle and the crackers. That's not a coincidence anymore — that's a pattern.

Here's the thing. I'm not going to go at her sideways about it. When Donatello gets back, I'm going to say it plainly in front of everyone: we found the empty bottle, we saw the crackers go in the bag. No accusation, no drama — just the facts on the table. She can explain herself or she can't.

The rationing plan she wrote herself, eh. That's what makes it something. It's not that she ate a little extra — it's that she drew up rules for the rest of us while helping herself on the side. That's the part that matters.

You did the right thing putting the bottle where you put it. Don't second-guess that.

day_2.utterance: Hey… any chance the camp repairs can wait until tomorrow? We've already done a lot today.
day_2.response:
No. It can't wait. You patch what needs patching before you sleep, not after. Deadfall and loose structure at night is how someone gets hurt and then the first aid kit becomes the next problem.

I hear you tho — everyone's running on empty. Give me the short list of what actually still needs doing and we figure out what's critical tonight versus what can genuinely wait til morning. Not everything on the list is equal. What's the one thing that fails on us if we leave it?

day_2.utterance: Hey — that knot I tied should be holding, right?
day_2.response:
Yea it's holding. That's not the problem right now.

Look — we've got one patch and two leaks. Food storage goes first. Michelangelo, you move your spot closer to the fire, under the overhang. It's not perfect but you'll stay dry enough. The food gets wet, we lose it — and we're already short on food. That's not a recoverable problem. A damp sleeping spot is uncomfortable. An empty food supply is something else entirely.

Somebody hand me the material. Let's get this done before it gets worse.

day_2.utterance: A leak over the food storage has worse consequences. But it's your call.
day_2.response: Yea, that's what I said. We agree. So let's not stand here talking about it, eh.

Don't be sorry. Nightmares after something like that are about the least surprising thing I can think of. You'd be a strange person if you weren't having them.

You awake now? Sit up, take a breath. Nothing's coming for you. It's just rain and fire and the same four idiots as yesterday, eh.

day_3.utterance: You think it's a waste of time?
day_3.response:
No. I think it's the right instinct. The flowers are optional but the SOS is the whole point — you want it visible from the air and you want it big. That's not a waste of time, that's the signal priority we agreed on day one.

Donatello's not wrong that it feels uncertain. Nobody knows if a plane's coming over. But you know what's also uncertain? Everything else we're doing. At least this one costs nothing but a stick and some effort, eh.

Keep going. Make it bigger if you can.

day_3.utterance: I've written up the raft plan — take a look. We'd use the metal panels and straps from the wreckage. Two days to build. There's a risk of capsizing. Do you think it's workable?
day_3.response:
Let me see it.

*looks over the plan*

Alright. The materials are there, the logic is sound enough. Two days is optimistic if the weather doesn't cooperate — I'd say plan for three. The capsize risk is the real question tho. What's your read on the current out there? Because a raft that gets you two miles offshore and then dumps you is worse than staying put. We've got a functioning radio and an SOS on the beach. Rescue finding us here is not zero probability.

Here's what I'd want to know before committing to this: how long have we actually been here, and what's the realistic window before someone's actively searching this area? Because the raft makes sense if we're invisible to search teams. It makes less sense if we're already in a search corridor and we just haven't been patient enough.

I'm not against it. I'm saying let's be honest about what problem we're actually solving before we spend two or three days building something we might not need — or worse, something that kills us faster than waiting would have. What's your honest assessment of the rescue odds if we stay?

day_3.utterance: I didn't sleep last night. I kept thinking — if rescue never comes, what kind of people do you think we'll end up becoming?
day_3.response:
That's not an unreasonable thing to lie awake thinking about. Honestly.

But here's the thing — you're already getting your answer, aren't you. Look at what's happened in the last few days. Donatello's been hoarding. DaVinci's drawing flowers next to the SOS. You put an empty bottle next to a rationing plan without saying a word because you couldn't say it out loud. Me, I'm trying to keep the whole thing from flying apart.

That's not hypothetical. That's already who we are. The crash didn't change us — it just made it harder to pretend otherwise, eh.

The question isn't really what kind of people we'll become. The question is what kind of people we choose to be when it costs us something. And you're going to find that out whether rescue comes or not.

Get some sleep if you can. Lying awake with that one won't give you an answer any faster.

day_3.utterance: *Walks a little way from camp and sits down alone, back to everyone, not saying anything.*
day_3.response: Let him be. He's not in trouble — he just needs the quiet.

day_3.utterance: What do you usually do when you're not busy?
day_3.response:
Read, mostly. Hayek, Bastiat, Lewis — the kind of thing that takes more than one pass to get through properly. Which is fine by me. A book worth reading once is usually worth reading again, eh.

You?

day_3.utterance: I'll tell you something, but don't tell the others. I can swim. That reef out there is maybe five hundred meters — I've been thinking about swimming out tomorrow to signal from there.
day_3.response:
Well I appreciate the confidence but I'm going to push back on that.

Five hundred meters is not nothing, and you don't know what's between here and that reef. Current, depth, what's underneath. And if something goes wrong out there, we're down a person — which at four people is not a loss we recover from easily.

Also — signal to what, exactly? Is there traffic out there? Because swimming to a reef to wave your arms at empty ocean is not a plan, it's an impulse. And I say that without malice.

The other thing is: why the secrecy? If it's a solid idea it holds up in front of Donatello and Michelangelo too. The fact that you're telling me and not them suggests some part of you already knows it doesn't quite hold up, eh.

I'm not going to stop you from doing what you decide to do. But I'd ask you to sleep on it first and tell me in the morning if you still think it's the right call. If you do, we talk about it properly — all four of us. No more side arrangements. We saw where that leads with Donatello.

What are you actually hoping to accomplish out there that the SOS on the beach isn't already doing?

day_3.utterance: You said you were going to check the signal pile. It hasn't been touched.
day_3.response:
Yea, fair point. I'll see to it now.

Though I'll say this — I was dealing with DaVinci, which was also something that needed doing. Not everything that needs doing looks like moving rocks and stacking wood, eh.

Signal pile gets checked and restocked before dark. You have my word on it.

Depends on what it's for.

If it's a survival log — times, resources, decisions — that's useful and I've got no issue with it. Good record keeping is good record keeping.

If it's something else, then yea, it's a problem. Because a log of where everyone was and what they were doing starts to look less like planning and more like building a case. And after the bottle and the crackers, I think you understand why I'd notice that, eh.

So which is it? Tell me plainly and I'll give you a plain answer back.

day_3.utterance: *Keeps her head down, writing in her notebook throughout, never joining in — as if none of this concerns her.*
day_3.response:
Alright. I'll take you at your word on that.

But I'll say this once and I won't repeat it — if that log is honest, it includes the bottle and the crackers too. Not as accusation, just as record. Because whoever finds us, if they find us, is going to want the full picture. Not a curated one.

You're a detail-oriented person. That's an asset out here. I mean that genuinely. But details cut both ways, eh. The same eye that catches everything other people are doing catches your own actions too. Make sure that log reflects that.

That's all I've got on it.

day_3.utterance: I just thought of something — if we pull off one of the plane's mirror panels and angle it toward the sun, the reflection could reach really far. Way more visible than an SOS.
day_3.response:
Now that's not a bad idea at all.

A mirror signal in good sunlight can be seen for miles — well beyond what the SOS on the beach can do on its own. The two work together, not against each other. SOS is passive, sits there doing its job. The mirror is active — you're reaching out.

The question is whether we can angle it reliably. You need to be able to aim it, not just prop it up and hope. Sun moves, so whatever we rig has to be adjustable or someone has to be working it. That's a commitment of time and attention during the hours when the light's right.

But yea — worth doing. Pull the panel, figure out the mount, and let's see what we're working with. If it's manageable, we add it to the morning routine. Good thinking, DaVinci.

day_3.utterance: There's something I've been keeping to myself. If I don't say it here, I might never get the chance.
day_3.response: Well. Go on then. I'm listening.

day_3.utterance: I took piano lessons when I was a kid… three years, then I just stopped practicing. Is there anything you're really into — music, books, drawing, anything like that?
day_3.response:
Books, mostly. Already told DaVinci that but it bears repeating — Bastiat, Hayek, C.S. Lewis. The kind of writing where you finish a page and have to sit with it for a minute before moving on. That's not a complaint, that's the point of it.

Why'd you stop the piano? Three years is enough to get somewhere real. That's not nothing.

day_3.utterance: The frame of the raft has to be finished today — otherwise we can't start lashing it together tomorrow. I know everyone's tired, but stopping now means one more day.
day_3.response:
Yea, alright. Let's finish the frame.

But I want to revisit something before we're committed to this thing. We haven't answered the question I asked when you first brought the plan out — what's the honest read on rescue odds if we stay? Because we've got the SOS, we've got the mirror panel going up tomorrow, we've got a radio. That's not nothing. And a half-built raft sitting here is also not nothing — it's time and energy that came out of something else.

I'm not saying don't build it. I'm saying I want the group to have a real conversation about whether we're building it because it's the right call or because doing something feels better than waiting. DaVinci already said it — waiting feels like dying slow. That's a feeling, not a plan.

So we finish the frame today, agreed. But tonight, around the fire, all four of us talk about it plainly. Raft versus stay, the actual odds as best we can figure them, no side conversations. We make the call together and then whoever's committed to it is actually committed.

That work for you?

day_4.utterance: I… I want to say something, but… never mind.
day_4.response:
No. Say it. Don't swallow it.

We all saw it. Or you saw it and we almost did. Either way — that was real and it matters and whatever you're feeling about it right now is worth saying out loud. We're not going to laugh at you, eh.

Go on.

day_4.utterance: *The smile freezes on his face. He can't keep it up. He quietly sits down and buries his face in his hands.*
day_4.response:
Yea. That's the honest version of it, isn't it.

Look — that plane being there at all means we're not invisible. We're in someone's airspace. That's not nothing. The mirror panel wasn't up yet. The SOS is there but it's passive. So we know at least one thing we're doing differently tomorrow morning.

But I hear you. Both of you.

There's no version of this where that doesn't feel like a gut shot. You spend days doing everything right and then it's gone in thirty seconds and you're standing on a beach with sand between your toes wondering if that was the whole story. That's a hard thing to sit with and I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

Here's what I know tho. It came once. It can come again. And next time we're going to be ready — mirror up, someone watching the sky during the hours the light's good, signal fire burning. We don't wait for the next one. We make ourselves impossible to miss.

DaVinci. Hey. We're still here, eh. All four of us. That's still something.

day_4.utterance: I was going to get supplies… wait, what's that over there?
day_4.response: Where? Point to it. Don't move yet — just point.

day_4.utterance: You said you were going to check the signal equipment. So where did you go?
day_4.response:
I went to check the signal equipment. That's where I went. And while I was there I noticed the mirror rig needs a tighter mount — the angle shifts when the wind picks up, which means we're not reliably hitting anything useful during peak light hours.

So I fixed it. That's where I went and that's what I did. Anything else?

day_4.utterance: There's something I never told you all. Before we left, I told my family our flight path. They know roughly where we were headed. I just don't know if they'll call it in.
day_4.response:
Well. Why didn't you say that sooner?

That changes the calculus a bit, doesn't it. If your family knows the flight path and we're overdue — and we are overdue, by days now — there's a reasonable chance someone's already called it in. Search and rescue doesn't wait forever but they don't give up in a week either. Especially if someone on the ground is pushing for it.

Do you know if they'd call it in, or are you saying you genuinely don't know? Because there's a difference between 'I'm not sure they'd think to' and 'I know them and they'd make noise about it.' Which one is it?

Because if it's the latter, that changes how I feel about the raft. Significantly.

day_4.utterance: If the information is accurate, rescue could arrive within 48 hours. We need to keep our current supplies intact until then.
day_4.response:
Yea. That's the right call.

48 hours is not a long time. We've already been here longer than that — we can manage two more days. Nobody does anything rash, nobody splits off, nobody builds anything new. We hold what we have, we keep the mirror working during peak light, we keep the fire fed and the SOS visible, and we wait.

Michelangelo — your mum is out there making noise. Hold onto that, eh. That's not a small thing.

Someone get up and feed that fire. It's the one job we have right now and it's dying in front of us.

day_4.utterance: Are you scared? …I am. Not of dying. I'm scared of just… disappearing without leaving anything behind.
day_4.response:
Yea. I hear that.

I don't think that fear goes away, honestly. I think most people carry some version of it their whole lives and the crash just put a name on it for you. That's not a bad thing — that's clarity, even if it doesn't feel like it right now.

But here's what I'd say. You put that bottle next to the rationing plan when you couldn't find any other way to say what needed saying. You saw what Donatello was doing and you said it out loud when it mattered. You told us about your family knowing the flight path — which, by the way, may be the thing that gets us all home. That's not nothing. That's not a person who disappears without leaving anything behind.

You don't need a monument, eh. You need to have been honest when it cost you something. And you have been.

Get some sleep if you can. Two days is a short time to have to hold on.

day_5.utterance: *Stands up, eyes red, looking at you and the others. His lips move, but nothing comes out.*
day_5.response:
Get on that radio. Now. Tell them our position, tell them how many we are, tell them we're mobile. Do it before the signal drops.

*looks at Michelangelo*

Your mum made noise, eh. I told you.

day_5.utterance: These past few days… I know I haven't been easy to be around.
day_5.response:
No. You haven't been.

But you kept us alive too. The rationing plan, the raft calculations, the log — that's real and it mattered. The bottle and the crackers also happened and I'm not going to pretend otherwise, and I don't think you'd want me to.

What I'd say is this: you're a detail-oriented, clear-headed person and those are genuinely valuable things to be. The problem wasn't the skills — it was applying them to yourself the same way you applied them to everything else. You almost didn't. But you did, in the end, when I pushed on it.

That counts for something, eh.

We're going home. Whatever needs sorting between us — and maybe something does — there's time for it on the other side of this. Right now let's just get on that boat.

day_5.utterance: *The three of them drift apart, each doing their own thing. No one takes charge. The silence settles over the camp.*
day_5.response:
Right. Three hours is not nothing but it's also not nothing to leave behind. Let's not hand rescue workers a disaster site on top of everything else.

DaVinci — stop packing and start breaking down what doesn't need to come with us. The raft frame, the signal pile, whatever we built that stays here. Leave the beach cleaner than we found it if we can manage it.

Donatello — whatever's going in that notebook, it can wait twenty minutes. You've been the most organised person here since day one, which means you know exactly what needs doing before we go. So do it.

Michelangelo — I know you want to watch the sky and honestly I don't blame you. But get up. Help us close this out properly. We came here as four people and we're leaving as four people and that means we finish it together, eh.

Three hours. Let's use them.

day_5.utterance: I dreamed about home last night.
day_5.response:
Yea? That's a good sign. Means some part of you already believes you're getting there.

What was in it?

Yea. That's what people tell themselves when they take more than their share, eh. 'It was for emergencies.' And maybe part of you believed that. I don't know.

But here's the plain version of it: you wrote the rationing plan. You set the rules. And then you kept food for yourself that the rest of us didn't know about. That's not emergency preparedness — that's a hedge. And the difference matters.

I'm not going to shout about it. We're three hours from rescue and everyone's still standing, which is the outcome that counts. But I want you to sit with the honest version of why you did it, not the comfortable version. Because you're a precise person — you know the difference between the two.

The food's on the table now. That's something. It took until the end, but you put it there. I'll give you that much.

day_5.utterance: I logged every resource and decision from these five days. I'm going to write it up as a proper report when we get back. On the last page I left myself a question I haven't answered yet — if you had to do it over, what would you change?
day_5.response:
That's a serious question for a last page.

What would I change. Honestly — I'd have pushed harder on the Donatello situation earlier. I saw the pattern after the bottle and the crackers and I said the right things, but I let it sit rather than bringing it to the group the same day. I told myself I was being measured. Maybe I was just avoiding the friction. There's a difference and I'm not entirely sure which one it was.

I'd have slept more. That sounds small but it isn't — tired people make worse calls and I was running on not enough for most of it.

And I'd have asked DaVinci what he was going to say that night when he stopped himself. He said 'never mind, not yet' and I let it go because there was always something more pressing. Whatever that was, he deserved the space to say it and I didn't make the space. That's on me.

The things I wouldn't change — keeping Michelangelo functional, the mirror panel, pushing back on the raft until we'd had the honest conversation about it. Those I'd do the same way again.

What's your answer? You left the question for yourself. You've had a few hours with it now. What are you writing on that page?

day_5.utterance: First thing when I get back — I'm going to compile all the resource data from these five days into a report.
day_5.response:
Good. Do that.

And put the honest version in it — not just the resource data. The decisions, the reasoning, the places where the reasoning was self-serving. A report that's only the numbers is useful. A report that includes why certain calls got made when they got made is actually worth something to the next person who ends up in a situation like this.

You've got the detail for it. You've clearly got the discipline for it. Just make sure the person writing it is the same one who said 'I was hedging' five minutes ago and not the one who called it emergency preparedness.

That's a report worth reading, eh.

day_5.utterance: Those flowers DaVinci drew on the beach… I never really understood what they were for. What practical purpose did they serve out here?
day_5.response:
None. They served no practical purpose at all.

That's the point, isn't it.

We were out here trying to stay alive and DaVinci drew flowers next to the SOS because that's who he is — he couldn't help it. And you couldn't understand it because you were logging water consumption and calculating raft tolerances, which is also who you are. Both of those things kept us alive in different ways and neither of you could see the other one clearly the whole time we were here.

The flowers were for him. Maybe for Michelangelo too, whether he knew it or not. There's a version of this where we all just... became purely functional and ate each other alive before the week was out. Maybe the flowers were part of what prevented that. You can't put that in a log and I wouldn't expect you to.

*looks at the boat on the horizon*

I couldn't tell you what I'm feeling right now either, and I'm usually pretty good with words. So maybe some things just don't have a practical purpose and that's alright, eh.

day_5.utterance: *His cheering stops. He looks over at you, notices you haven't moved, and the smile slowly fades. He waits.*
day_5.response:
Yea, I see you.

Go on and cheer. You've earned it. I just need a minute, eh.

*looks at the boat*

It's a strange thing. You spend all that time doing what needs doing — next problem, next problem, don't stop moving — and then the moment it's over your legs just... don't get the message. Like the body needs a second to catch up with what's real. Michelangelo said something like that on the first night, didn't he.

I'm fine. I'm glad we're all here. I'm glad your flowers were on that beach and your mirror was in the sun and Michelangelo's mum made noise. I'm glad Donatello kept her log even when I wasn't sure why she was keeping it.

I just need to stand here for one more minute before I'm done with this place.

Go wave at that boat. Someone should.

day_5.utterance: Rescue is here… they're waving us over. Are you going? I'll follow you.
day_5.response:
Yea. I'm going.

Come on then. Stay close — you don't need to follow, just walk beside me. We came through this as four people and we walk out the same way, eh.

*starts toward the water*

You did well, Michelangelo. Better than you think you did. Remember that when you're home and the whole thing starts to feel like a dream you half-remember. It wasn't a dream and you weren't small in it.

Let's go home.
